subject: Neurology
vignette: A 9-year-old child has a lesion affecting the inferior cerebellar peduncle. During examination, the physician notes that the child cannot coordinate movements on the same side of the body when the eyes are closed, despite intact conscious sensation. Proprioceptive information from the spinal cord reaches the cerebellum through this peduncle.
question: Which of the following best describes the proprioceptive information carried by the inferior cerebellar peduncle?

options.text: Contralateral conscious proprioception to the cerebellum
Ipsilateral conscious proprioception to the cerebral cortex
Ipsilateral unconscious proprioception from the spinal cord to the cerebellum
Contralateral unconscious proprioception from the cortex via Purkinje cells
Vestibular input exclusively to the flocculonodular lobe

explanation_correct: The inferior cerebellar peduncle carries ipsilateral (unconscious) proprioceptive information from the spinal cord to the cerebellum. This input allows the cerebellum to modulate movement and coordinate posture without conscious perception, so a lesion causes ipsilateral incoordination. This is a key afferent pathway for cerebellar modulation of movement.

explanation_incorrect.A: The inferior peduncle carries ipsilateral, unconscious rather than contralateral conscious proprioception.
explanation_incorrect.B: Conscious proprioception ascends to the cerebral cortex via the dorsal columns and medial lemniscus, not through the inferior cerebellar peduncle.
explanation_incorrect.D: Contralateral cortical input reaches the cerebellum via the middle cerebellar peduncle (corticopontocerebellar fibers), not the inferior peduncle.
explanation_incorrect.E: Vestibular nuclei do project to the flocculonodular lobe, but the defining role tested here is spinal unconscious proprioception carried by the inferior peduncle.

educationalObjective: Recall that the inferior cerebellar peduncle carries ipsilateral unconscious proprioception from the spinal cord.

subject: Neurology
vignette: A neuroanatomy student is learning the order of the cerebellar deep nuclei from lateral to medial. She recalls the mnemonic "don't eat greasy foods" and wants to correctly list the nuclei and match them to the vermis (medial) versus the hemispheres (lateral).
question: Which of the following lists the cerebellar deep nuclei in correct order from lateral to medial?

options.text: Dentate, emboliform, globose, fastigial
Fastigial, globose, emboliform, dentate
Dentate, globose, emboliform, fastigial
Emboliform, dentate, fastigial, globose
Globose, fastigial, dentate, emboliform

explanation_correct: The deep cerebellar nuclei from lateral to medial are dentate, emboliform, globose, and fastigial, remembered by the mnemonic "don't eat greasy foods" (Dentate, Emboliform, Globose, Fastigial). The laterally placed dentate nucleus is associated with the cerebellar hemispheres, while the medially placed fastigial nucleus is associated with the vermis.

explanation_incorrect.B: This is the reverse (medial-to-lateral) order: fastigial, globose, emboliform, dentate.
explanation_incorrect.C: This swaps globose and emboliform; the correct order places emboliform before globose.
explanation_incorrect.D: This order incorrectly places emboliform before dentate and fastigial before globose.
explanation_incorrect.E: This order incorrectly places globose and fastigial laterally before dentate and emboliform.

educationalObjective: Order the deep cerebellar nuclei from lateral to medial using "don't eat greasy foods".

subject: Neurology
vignette: A 54-year-old man has a tumor compressing the midline vermis of the cerebellum. He has difficulty maintaining truncal balance and coordinating both proximal limbs, but his distal finger movements are relatively preserved. A separate patient has a lateral hemispheric lesion causing ipsilateral distal limb incoordination.
question: Which of the following best contrasts the functions of the medial (vermis) and lateral (hemispheric) cerebellum?

options.text: Vermis controls distal ipsilateral limbs; hemispheres control axial muscles bilaterally
Vermis controls ipsilateral distal limbs; hemispheres control contralateral axial muscles
Both vermis and hemispheres control distal muscles ipsilaterally
Vermis controls contralateral axial muscles; hemispheres control ipsilateral proximal muscles
Vermis controls axial and proximal limb musculature bilaterally; hemispheres control distal limb musculature ipsilaterally

explanation_correct: The medial cerebellum (vermis) controls axial and proximal limb musculature bilaterally, which is why a midline vermal lesion causes truncal and bilateral proximal ataxia. The lateral cerebellar hemispheres control distal limb musculature ipsilaterally, so a hemispheric lesion produces ipsilateral distal incoordination.

explanation_incorrect.A: This reverses the roles; the vermis controls axial and proximal muscle bilaterally, not distal ipsilateral limbs.
explanation_incorrect.B: The vermis is not concerned with ipsilateral distal limbs, and the hemispheres are ipsilateral (not contralateral) for distal control.
explanation_incorrect.C: This incorrectly assigns distal muscle control to both regions; only the hemispheres control distal musculature.
explanation_incorrect.D: The vermis acts bilaterally, not contralaterally, and the hemispheres govern distal rather than proximal muscles.

educationalObjective: Contrast vermal (axial/proximal, bilateral) with hemispheric (distal, ipsilateral) cerebellar control.

subject: Neurology
vignette: A 19-year-old patient with suspected cerebellar dysfunction undergoes neurologic testing. The examiner notes a tremor that worsens as the patient's finger approaches a target, difficulty performing rapid alternating pronation and supination, and an unsteady gait.
question: Which of the following findings is most characteristic of cerebellar dysfunction?

options.text: Resting tremor that improves with voluntary movement
Intention tremor with impaired rapid alternating movements
Loss of two-point discrimination with intact coordination
Spastic paralysis with hyperreflexia
Decreased vibration sense in a stocking distribution

explanation_correct: Cerebellar function is tested with rapid alternating movements (pronation/supination), finger-to-nose, heel-to-shin, and gait. An intention tremor, one that worsens as the target is approached, along with dysdiadochokinesia (impaired rapid alternating movements) and a wide-based ataxic gait, is classic for cerebellar disease.

explanation_incorrect.A: A resting tremor that improves with movement is characteristic of Parkinson disease (basal ganglia), not cerebellar dysfunction.
explanation_incorrect.C: Loss of two-point discrimination reflects somatosensory cortex or dorsal column pathology, not the cerebellum.
explanation_incorrect.D: Spastic paralysis with hyperreflexia indicates an upper motor neuron lesion, not cerebellar ataxia.
explanation_incorrect.E: Stocking-distribution sensory loss indicates a peripheral neuropathy, not a cerebellar lesion.

educationalObjective: Identify intention tremor and impaired rapid alternating movements as key cerebellar signs.
